description: Estimation, scheduling, risks, prototypes, and teamwork.

screens.body:
A project plan starts by breaking work down. 'Build the checkout' is not a task — it's a wish. Break it until each piece is small enough to estimate: 'design checkout screen,' 'write payment API call,' 'test card-declined flow.'

A good task takes hours to a few days and has a clear done. If you can't say when it's finished, break it smaller. This breakdown is called a work breakdown structure — a fancy name for a to-do list with sub-bullets.

options: Break it into small tasks with a clear 'done'
Estimate the whole thing as one number
check.question: 'Build the checkout' is too big. You…

screens.heading: Break it down
screens.keyPoint: If you can't say when it's done, break it smaller.

screens.body:
Estimates are guesses with structure. Story points compare task sizes relatively (this is twice that). T-shirt sizes (S/M/L/XL) do the same with less math. Always estimate as a range, not a single confident number.

Then add buffer for the unknown — things will go wrong. A plan with no slack is a plan that fails on the first surprise. Under-promise, over-deliver.

options: A single exact number of hours
Whatever the client wants to hear
A range, plus buffer for surprises
check.question: A healthy estimate is…

screens.heading: Estimating effort
screens.keyPoint: Estimate in ranges, reveal together, keep buffer.

screens.body:
A schedule is tasks plus time: milestones (big checkpoints like 'beta ready'), dependencies ('API before UI'), and a timeline. The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks — it decides the earliest possible finish.

Watch the critical path like a hawk. A delay on a critical task delays the project; a delay elsewhere just eats slack. That's where your attention belongs.

options: The longest chain of dependent tasks
check.question: The critical path is…

screens.heading: Scheduling
screens.keyPoint: The critical path decides your finish date.

screens.body:
Every task needs exactly one owner. Shared ownership means nobody owns it. Assign people to tasks and milestones based on skills and availability — not wishful thinking about who's free.

Write the assignments down where everyone can see them: a board, a doc, a tracker. 'I thought you were doing that' is the most expensive sentence in project management.
screens.heading: Who does what
screens.keyPoint: One owner per task, written down visibly.

screens.body:
A risk is a maybe-problem. For each one, score likelihood × impact (both 1–5): a 5×5 risk needs a plan today; a 1×1 risk gets a shrug. Then define mitigations (reduce the chance) and contingencies (what you do if it happens anyway).

Review risks regularly — new ones appear, old ones fade. The team that names its fears handles them; the team that doesn't gets ambushed.

options: Score likelihood × impact, then plan mitigations
check.question: When you spot a project risk…

screens.heading: Risks
screens.keyPoint: Score them, mitigate the big ones, review often.

screens.body:
A UI prototype is a clickable mock — Figma is the standard tool — that looks like the app but does nothing real. It lets clients react to the design before anyone codes. A system prototype is the opposite: ugly, but it proves the hardest technical piece actually works.

Build the UI prototype to validate the design, and the system prototype to kill the scariest technical risk. Both are cheaper than building the wrong thing.

options: A clickable mock to validate design early
check.question: A UI prototype is…

screens.heading: Prototypes
screens.keyPoint: Prototype the design AND the scariest technical risk.

screens.body:
Plans don't execute themselves — teams do. Effective teams communicate in rhythms: daily standups for blockers, reviews for demos, retrospectives for improving how they work. Decisions get written down, not lost in chat scroll.

Professional practices seal it: code reviews, shared coding standards, respectful disagreement, and owning mistakes. The best plan with a dysfunctional team still fails.

options: One big meeting at the start
check.question: Healthy team communication means…

screens.heading: Teamwork that works
screens.keyPoint: Rhythms plus professional habits beat heroics.

screens.body: The Scrum Guide — scrum.org. Figma's official help and tutorials — help.figma.com. (For estimation deep-dives, search 'planning poker' — it's a team game, not a solo guess.)
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: Practice planning poker with your team.

title: Project Planning
